newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Business looks to Tung for smooth HK transition.
newsitem.headline: Business looks to Tung for smooth HK transition.

text.p: The world's business community welcomed the selection of one of their own on Wednesday as Hong Kong's future leader.
International shipping tycoon Tung Chee-hwa won 320 votes cast by the 400-member Selection Committee set up by China to choose Hong Kong's post-colonial leadership.
"With Tung Chee-hwa in the leadership position, Hong Kong will have the most pro-business government in recent history," said Janet Gilles, sales director at OCBC Securities.

His victory was widely expected and was likely to underpin the confidence of both local and international business people that capitalist Hong Kong will be integrated as smoothly as possible into communist China after midnight on June 30, 1997.

"The priority of Mr Tung and the people that will be coming in will be to create the impression that Hong Kong is having a smooth transition and the fundamentals that have made Hong Kong a prosperous economy are going to continue after 1997," Steve Taran of Lehman Brothers told Reuters Financial Television.
Tung's support in the local business community was virtually assured -- one-fourth of the Selection Committee was drawn largely from the cream of the business and financial sectors.

"Mr Tung's extensive business background, his service to the local community and his widespread contacts in China and internationally will serve him well as chief executive," the Hong Kong General Chamber of Commerce said in a statement.
Overseas business was also likely to be pleased, given Tung's extensive experience in the international arena as former head of his family-controlled shipping firm, Orient Overseas.

"We know him well, he's a very experienced international business executive and I think he understands the importance of international business to the future prosperity of Hong Kong," said President Frank Martin of the American Chamber of Commerce.
The stock market rose early as investors took comfort in prospects for a smooth transition following Tung's victory, although it tumbled later on interest rate-related fears.
The Hang Seng index surged 130 points in morning trade as Tung took the vote, but closed down 152.86 points at 13,189.60.
Nonetheless, Tung will have a big job keeping the confidence of the local and international business communities and working with a sovereign that has a vastly different economic system.

Hong Kong's population and size may be miniscule against China's vast bulk, but the territory is an economic powerhouse, the world's eighth-largest trading entity and a banking and financial centre of global importance.
Its per capita gross domestic product (GDP) at US$23,000 in 1995 is 10 times China's, and its government is one of the richest in the world with foreign reserves of US$62 billion.

The central government in Beijing has promised not to interfere in Hong Kong's capitalist system for 50 years under its "one country, two systems" policy, and Tung has vowed to take a hard line against meddling by local Chinese officials.

But while business people are fairly confident that Hong Kong will maintain its independence in economic policy, they are remain unsure that China understands the importance to business of issues such as rule of law and press freedom.
Some question whether Beijing annointed Tung because he does not have a major power base in Hong Kong and because it bailed him out when his business ran into trouble a decade ago.

"This man was not particularly well known before his name surfaced as the leading candidate, his career as a businessman was very much inherited from his father," consultant Philip Bowring told Reuters Financial Television.

But the American Chamber's Martin said Tung was well aware of the importance of laws and freedoms. "I've known Mr Tung for 20 years, there's no question in my mind he has the character to stand up for what is best for Hong Kong," he said.
